name: Vulnerability Discovery
description: Finding vulnerabilities at scale, CVE/patch analysis, bug bounties, and disclosure processes.

uss.narrative:
The earliest USENIX Security work in this set attacked two persistent hard problems: automatic exploit generation and patch-presence verification. teEther (USENIX 2018) showed that Ethereum smart-contract vulnerabilities could be found and exploited fully automatically from bytecode alone, while FUZE (USENIX 2018) tackled the notoriously manual process of assessing whether a kernel use-after-free bug was actually exploitable. On the defensive side, Precise and Accurate Patch Presence Test for Binaries (USENIX 2018) gave defenders a way to audit binaries for missing patches without source code — a problem that mattered enormously for vendor firmware. Concurrently, the community began systematizing vulnerability knowledge: Understanding the Reproducibility of Crowd-reported Security Vulnerabilities (USENIX 2018) and Towards the Detection of Inconsistencies in Public Security Vulnerability Reports (USENIX 2019) audited the CVE/NVD ecosystem itself and exposed how unreliable public disclosures could be.

A productive second wave through 2020–2021 pushed automated discovery across new surfaces. Fuzzing matured rapidly: GREYONE (USENIX 2020) introduced data-flow-sensitive mutation to break through hard-to-reach paths, FuzzGen (USENIX 2020) automated the creation of library fuzz drivers by mining consumer code, and Montage (USENIX 2020) applied neural language models to guide JavaScript engine fuzzing — one of the first ML-steered fuzzers at USENIX. MVP (USENIX 2020) tackled recurring vulnerabilities by matching code against patch-enhanced signatures. Firmware became a major front: PARTEMU, FIRMSCOPE, and Jetset (USENIX 2020–2021) progressively improved dynamic and static analysis for the deeply embedded software that traditional toolchains could not reach.

The 2022–2023 period broadened scope to multi-language and multi-component software. PolyCruise (USENIX 2022) crossed language boundaries with dynamic information-flow analysis, Mining Node.js Vulnerabilities (USENIX 2022) caught prototype-pollution and command-injection bugs in npm packages via an object dependence graph, and Fuzztruction (USENIX 2023) attacked structured-data parsers by fault-injecting generator programs rather than mutating raw bytes. Graph-based deep learning arrived with VulChecker (USENIX 2023), which localized vulnerable lines in source code rather than just flagging files. V1SCAN (USENIX 2023) addressed the supply-chain dimension by finding 1-day vulnerabilities in reused open-source components at scale.

By 2024–2025, large language models transformed the field again. PentestGPT (USENIX 2024) demonstrated that LLMs could reason across penetration-testing tasks end to end, and Cascade (USENIX 2024) showed CPU silicon itself was fuzzable with intricate program generation. Patch repair closed the loop: Logs In, Patches Out (USENIX 2025) and PATCHAGENT (USENIX 2025) used tree-of-thought LLM reasoning to generate working patches from sanitizer logs and source code alone, completing the arc from discovery to remediation inside a single automated pipeline.

ndss.narrative:
Vulnerability discovery at NDSS has followed the maturation of fuzzing and program analysis as primary methodologies, while expanding from desktop software to firmware and protocol implementations. Automated Generation of Event-Oriented Exploits in Android Hybrid Apps (NDSS 2018) showed that mobile hybrid apps introduce unique exploit primitives not covered by traditional web or native analysis. REDQUEEN (NDSS 2019) then demonstrated that input-to-state correspondence could bypass magic-byte and checksum filters that stalled coverage-guided fuzzers, opening deep code paths without expensive symbolic execution.

The 2020–2021 period targeted the kernel and cellular firmware. HFL (NDSS 2020) combined symbolic execution and fuzzing to find Linux kernel vulnerabilities; BaseSpec (NDSS 2021) discovered baseband bugs by comparing cellular L3 firmware implementations against their specifications—a form of differential analysis that proved highly effective for finding specification-conformance vulnerabilities.

By 2023–2025 cross-architecture and LLM-assisted discovery had become central. VulHawk (NDSS 2023) performed cross-architecture code search using entropy-based embeddings; Faster and Better (NDSS 2024) improved IoT firmware vulnerability detection; and From Large to Mammoth (NDSS 2025) ran a comparative evaluation of multiple LLMs on vulnerability discovery tasks, beginning the scientific process of understanding where language models genuinely help and where they fail.

top4.narrative:
The earliest papers here, all from 2018, reflect a field organized around two poles. On one side, coverage-guided fuzzing was maturing fast: "Angora: Efficient Fuzzing by Principled Search" (S&P 2018), "CollAFL: Path Sensitive Fuzzing" (S&P 2018), and "T-Fuzz: Fuzzing by Program Transformation" (S&P 2018) each attacked a different bottleneck — input search, coverage path collisions, and code that blocks shallow inputs — while "Evaluating Fuzz Testing" (CCS 2018) forced the community to confront how sloppy fuzzer benchmarking had become. On the other side, a human- and process-oriented strand emerged: "Hackers vs. Testers" (S&P 2018) compared how people actually find bugs, and "Understanding the Reproducibility of Crowd-reported Security Vulnerabilities" (USENIX 2018) and "Enter the Hydra" (USENIX 2018) probed crowd reports and bug-bounty incentives. New target domains also opened up, notably smart contracts in "teEther" (USENIX 2018).

Across 2019 and 2020 the fuzzing work got sharper and more specialized. "REDQUEEN" (NDSS 2019) cracked magic-byte and checksum barriers cheaply, "NAUTILUS" (NDSS 2019) and "CodeAlchemist" (NDSS 2019) brought grammars and semantics to deeply structured targets like language interpreters and JavaScript engines, and "ProFuzzer" (S&P 2019) inferred input structure on the fly. Fuzzing then spread to harder substrates — kernel races in "Razzer" (S&P 2019), the LTE control plane in "Touching the Untouchables" (S&P 2019), database engines in "SQUIRREL" (CCS 2020), and embedded firmware in "Karonte" (S&P 2020) — while "FuzzGen" (USENIX 2020) automated the harness-writing that had gated library fuzzing. Performance and guidance also advanced through "Full-Speed Fuzzing" (S&P 2019), "GREYONE" (USENIX 2020), and hybrid fuzzing/concolic combinations in "SAVIOR" (S&P 2020) and "HFL" (NDSS 2020).

Alongside the fuzzers, a distinct measurement-and-disclosure track took shape: "Towards the Detection of Inconsistencies in Public Security Vulnerability Reports" (USENIX 2019) and "MVP: Detecting Vulnerabilities using Patch-Enhanced Vulnerability Signatures" (USENIX 2020) treated CVE/NVD data and patches themselves as objects of analysis, supporting recurring-bug detection at scale. The smart-contract line kept its own momentum from "teEther" (2018) through "ETHBMC" (USENIX 2020) and "SmarTest" (USENIX 2021), which notably reached for language-model guidance to steer symbolic execution.

By 2022-2024 the center of gravity shifts twice. Directed fuzzing matures with provable pruning in "BEACON" (S&P 2022), but the larger inflection is the arrival of large language models. "Examining Zero-Shot Vulnerability Repair with Large Language Models" (S&P 2023) asks whether LLMs can fix the bugs the field has spent years finding, "PentestGPT" (USENIX 2024) harnesses them for offensive testing, and "LLMs Cannot Reliably Identify and Reason About Security Vulnerabilities (Yet?)" (S&P 2024) supplies the sober benchmark, echoing the same evaluation-rigor concern that "Evaluating Fuzz Testing" raised back in 2018. The area today therefore spans automated discovery (fuzzing/symbolic), data-driven patch and CVE analysis, and an open, contested question of how far LLMs can carry discovery, repair, and disclosure.
